h1: Measuring brand awareness for a small brewery without a research agency
title: Measuring Brewery Brand Awareness | Craft Beer School
desc: Practical ways for a small brewery to measure brand awareness without an agency: recall surveys, search data, till questions and social signals.
teaser: You do not need a research agency to know whether people have heard of you. You need a clipboard, a free search tool and some discipline.
standfirst: Awareness is the first thing a brand needs and the hardest thing for a small brewery to see. We show cheap, honest ways to measure it and how to read the numbers without fooling yourself.
sections:
Brand awareness is simply the share of your target drinkers who know your brewery exists. Marketers split it two ways:

  • Unaided recall. Ask "Which craft breweries in Pune can you name?" and count how many mention you without a prompt.
  • Aided recognition. Show a list of names or logos and ask "Which of these have you heard of?"

Recognition is always higher than recall. A brewery that people recognise but cannot name is known but not top of mind. That gap tells you something useful about where to spend your next rupee.

Big brewers pay agencies for large samples. A small brewery can get a rough but useful read with a short survey of real drinkers in its area. Keep it to four or five questions:

  1. Which craft breweries or brewpubs in this city can you name?
  2. Which of these have you heard of? (Show your name among six to eight others.)
  3. Have you tried beer from any of them?
  4. Where did you hear about the ones you know?

Ask in places where your target drinkers are but you are not: a food festival, a different taproom's quiz night with permission, an office group in a tech park. Asking in your own taproom only measures people who already know you.

Be realistic about sample size. With about 100 responses, a result like 30% recognition has a margin of error of roughly plus or minus nine percentage points. That is enough to see big shifts year to year, not small ones. Run the same survey, the same way, at the same time each year.
Use the free search and social data you already have

People who know your name search for it. Several free tools show this:

  • Google Search Console shows how often your brewery's name is searched and clicked through to your site.
  • Your Google Business Profile shows how many people found you by searching your name versus a category like "brewery near me".
  • Google Trends can show search interest over time if your name gets enough searches.
  • Instagram insights show profile visits and reach from non-followers, a rough signal of how far your name is travelling.

Track branded searches monthly. A steady rise over a year, after you allow for seasonal patterns such as the drop many places see in the monsoon, is one of the best cheap signals that awareness is growing.
Ask at the till and the door

The simplest data is often the most reliable. Train staff to ask new customers one question: "How did you hear about us?" Keep a tally on a sheet behind the bar or a field in your POS. After three months you will know whether word of mouth, Instagram, Zomato, a festival or a delivery app is doing the work.

Watch the share of first-time visitors too. If awareness is growing, new faces should be a steady part of each week, not only regulars.

Small data is easy to over-read. A few cautions:

  • One spike in branded searches after a news story is not lasting awareness. Look at the trend over months.
  • Followers can be bought or inflated by giveaways. Reach from non-followers and saves are better signals.
  • Survey answers are shaped by where you ask. Note the location and keep it consistent.
  • Awareness is not preference. People may know your name and still choose someone else. Ask about trial too.

Combine three or four measures rather than trusting one. If survey recognition, branded search and "heard from a friend" at the till all rise together, you can believe it.

Measurement only matters if it changes what you do. If recognition is decent but recall is low, your name is not sticky enough: look at naming, distinctiveness and repetition. If almost nobody has heard of you outside your neighbourhood, the job is reach, through festivals, collaborations or distribution. A brewery brand audit helps you see which.

Set awareness goals the same way you would set goals for a rebrand: a baseline, a target and a date. Then repeat the measurement and see whether you moved.
faqs: How many people should a brewery survey for brand awareness?
About 100 responses gives a rough read with a margin of roughly nine percentage points. Keep the method the same each year so changes are comparable.
What is the difference between recall and recognition?
Recall is naming your brand unprompted. Recognition is knowing it when shown a list. Recognition is always higher.
Is follower count a good measure of awareness?
Not on its own, because followers can be inflated. Branded searches, reach to non-followers and till answers are more reliable signals.
